One treatment, one mediator, one outcome: the model behind most mediation
analyses. This page runs it three ways and reads the result. Part of the
[Models](models.html) collection; for a one-page lookup see the
[Reference Card](refcard.html).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Structure** | X to M to Y, with the direct path X to Y |
| **Class returned** | `MediationData` |
| **Indirect effect** | $a \, b$ |
| **Routes** | `med()`, `fit_mediation()`, `extract_mediation()` on `lm`/`glm`, lavaan, or `fit_sem()` |

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(medfit)
library(generics)
covs <- c("covariate1", "covariate2")
```

## When to use it

Use it when one mediator carries the effect of the treatment and you have no
reason to expect a treatment-by-mediator interaction. If the mediator and the
outcome interact with the treatment, see [interaction](model-interaction.html);
for two or more mediators see [serial](model-serial.html) and
[parallel](model-parallel.html).

## Route 1: one line

`med()` fits both models, extracts the structure and returns the result.

```{r}
#| label: route-med
res <- med(mediation_demo, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1",
           outcome = "outcome", covariates = covs)
quick(res)
```

## Route 2: formulas

`fit_mediation()` takes one formula per model, so each model can carry its own
covariates.

```{r}
#| label: route-fit
fit <- fit_mediation(
  formula_y = outcome ~ treatment + mediator1 + covariate1 + covariate2,
  formula_m = mediator1 ~ treatment + covariate1 + covariate2,
  data = mediation_demo, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1"
)
tidy(fit, type = "effects", conf_int = TRUE)
```

## Route 3: models you already fitted

```{r}
#| label: route-extract
fit_m <- lm(mediator1 ~ treatment + covariate1 + covariate2, mediation_demo)
fit_y <- lm(outcome ~ treatment + mediator1 + covariate1 + covariate2,
            mediation_demo)
x <- extract_mediation(fit_m, model_y = fit_y,
                       treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1")
paths(x)
```

The same object comes from a lavaan fit (`extract_mediation(lavaan_fit, ...)`)
or from the native engine (`extract_mediation(fit_sem(...), ...)`); see
[Cookbook recipe 10](cookbook.html#i-use-lavaan) and
[recipe 11](cookbook.html#a-latent-mediator-native-engine).

## Reading the result

| Quantity | Call | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `a` | `paths(x)` | effect of the treatment on the mediator |
| `b` | `paths(x)` | effect of the mediator on the outcome, holding the treatment fixed |
| `c_prime` | `paths(x)`, `nde(x)` | direct effect of the treatment |
| NIE | `nie(x)` | indirect effect, $a \, b$ |
| TE | `te(x)` | total effect, NIE plus NDE |
| PM | `pm(x)` | proportion mediated, NIE over TE |

```{r}
#| label: effects
c(nie = unname(nie(x)), nde = unname(nde(x)), te = unname(te(x)),
  pm = unname(pm(x)))
```

Intervals for the effects come from the delta method (`tidy()`, `confint()`).
For a bootstrap interval see [Bootstrap Inference](bootstrap.html).

## Assumptions and limits

- The treatment is randomized, or the models adjust for every confounder of the
  treatment-outcome, treatment-mediator and mediator-outcome relations.
- The mediator-outcome confounders must be in **both** models; leaving a
  covariate out of one biases that path.
- A near-zero total effect makes the proportion mediated unstable.
- The default `glm` engine is maximum likelihood on independent observations;
  for clustered data see
  [Cookbook recipe 9](cookbook.html#cluster-randomized-trial).
